title: Morning or Night
description: Sweep the hour hand twice round a day, find noon and midnight, and drop each time on its morning or evening half.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: See that a day is two rounds of the hour hand and so has 24 hours, name 12 o'clock in the day noon and 12 o'clock at night midnight, and write a time with a.m. before noon and p.m. after it.
writeup.look: A day strip from midnight to midnight with a sky blue morning half and an amber evening half, a wall clock above it, a sun and a moon, picture cards, a time card with a.m. and p.m. buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Morning or Night' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many times have been placed on the day strip. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A day strip runs across the working area at x 90, y 420, 1000 by 120, from midnight at the left end to midnight at the right end with noon at its middle. The left half, from midnight to noon, is a sky blue band labelled a.m., and the right half, from noon to midnight, is an amber band labelled p.m. Near-black tick marks stand at the ends and the middle, labelled midnight, noon and midnight. A sunrise over a small school is painted at x 130, y 300, a high sun at the middle at x 560, y 290, and a moon over a street lamp at x 130, y 560 and again at x 1000, y 560. A wall clock hangs at x 90, y 210, 190 across, drawn exactly, with a short vermilion hour hand and a long deep blue minute hand and no arrowheads, and a Sun slider under the strip at x 320, y 600, 520 wide, carries a small sun along the strip while the hands of the clock turn with it, the hour hand going twice round from end to end. Picture cards, an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football, a dinner plate and a bed, each 90 across, wait at x 320, y 214 and are dragged onto the strip. The time card stands at x 330, y 650, 300 by 90, and takes a time from the pad. The a.m. button and the p.m. button stand at x 660, y 650 and x 780, y 650, each 100 by 60, and the Noon and midnight button at x 900, y 650, 190 by 60. A green Answer tag at x 840, y 214, 250 by 70, holds what the child has written. The Plain clock button stands at x 110, y 650, 160 by 60. In the plain view the wall clock is drawn as a bare dial. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the hours and then the minutes of a time into the time card. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The time card shows the last time written in full beside its picture, with the day strip lit on the half it belongs to.

phases.win: the second round ends, the day strip fills from end to end and a green tag reads one whole day
phases.does: turns the hour hand once round, then a second time, and counts the hours of each round
phases.goal: the hour hand goes round the clock twice in a day, twelve hours and twelve hours, so a day has twenty-four hours
phases.says: Turn the hour hand round the clock. How many times does it go round in a day?
phases.check: Away from the screen: the short hand of a clock has gone round three times. How many days have passed, and why not three?
phases.feels: the hour hand sweeping round twice while the sun crosses the whole strip
phases.hands: Hold up a real clock or a paper plate clock, turn the short hand all the way round twice, and count the hours of each round aloud, ending with the hours in all.
phases.tries: First rung: count the rounds of the hour hand aloud. Second rung: say how many hours one round is. Third rung: the same task with one round only, before the second round is added.

wrong.why: one round of the face is the only round a child sees
wrong.move: says a day has 12 hours because the clock face shows 12 numbers
wrong.screen: the hour hand is turned a second time while the sun is still crossing the strip, and the second round is counted in amber beside the first in vermilion until the strip is full

wrong.why: the sun looks as if it has done most of its work by the middle
wrong.move: counts only the hours of the first round and stops at noon
wrong.screen: the strip stays unfilled from the middle to the far end, a gap labelled Still to come, and the hand is turned on until the gap closes

phases.screen: a day strip from one midnight to the next with a wall clock above it and its hour hand waiting at the twelve
phases.soWhat: the hour hand goes round twice in a day, so a day has 24 hours

phases.win: the middle of the strip lights as noon and the two ends light as midnight, with no label beside them
phases.does: slides the sun to the middle and to each end and names the twelve o'clock there noon or midnight
phases.goal: twelve o'clock in the day is noon and twelve o'clock at night is midnight, and neither takes a.m. or p.m.
phases.says: Both hands are at the twelve. Is the sun high, or is the moon out?
phases.check: Away from the screen: it is 12 o'clock and the street is dark and quiet. Is it noon or midnight, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the two twelves looking the same on the clock and different in the sky
phases.hands: Put a paper plate clock with both hands at the twelve beside two pictures, a bright sun and a dark night, and ask which picture goes with which twelve.
phases.tries: First rung: look at the sky and say if it is day or night. Second rung: say the word for 12 o'clock in the day and the word for 12 o'clock at night. Third rung: the same task with only the sun on the strip, before the moon returns.

wrong.why: both look the same on the clock face, so they get the same name
wrong.screen: the sun is dragged to the end of the strip and the sky goes dark, the moon comes out over the street lamp, and the label changes to midnight

wrong.why: every time of a day has had a label so far, so noon seems to need one too
wrong.move: writes a.m. or p.m. after noon or midnight
wrong.screen: the label buttons grey out on noon and midnight, and the card reads noon or midnight alone with a small note that it stands alone

phases.screen: the day strip with a high sun over the middle and a moon over a street lamp at each end, and both hands at the twelve
phases.soWhat: 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight, and neither takes a.m. or p.m.

phases.win: the card settles in its half and the label a.m. or p.m. lights beside it; the time card is written in full beside the picture and the day strip lights the half it belongs to
phases.does: drops a time or a picture card on the sky blue half or the amber half and says a.m. or p.m. types the time for a picture card, chooses a.m. or p.m., or chooses noon or midnight, and reads it back
phases.goal: from midnight to noon is a.m. and from noon to midnight is p.m. a time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, and noon and midnight are written as words with no label
phases.says: Is it before noon or after noon? Drop it on its half. Type the time. Then choose a.m. or p.m., or noon or midnight.
phases.check: Away from the screen: you eat breakfast and you eat dinner. Which is a.m. and which is p.m., and where is noon between them? Away from the screen: say a time in the evening and write it with its label. Then say the same hour in the morning and write that too. How are they different?
phases.feels: the strip split at noon, the sky blue half on one side and the amber half on the other; the time card finishing only when a label or a word is chosen
phases.hands: Colour a long paper strip sky blue on the left half and amber on the right half, mark noon in the middle, and ask each child to stick a picture of their own day on it and say a.m. or p.m. Write the time of a favourite part of the day on a card, then write a.m. or p.m. after it, and swap cards with a partner to check.
phases.tries: First rung: say whether the thing happens before or after noon. Second rung: drop the card on that half. Third rung: the same task with a time near the middle of the strip, before the times near the ends return. First rung: say which half of the day the time is in. Second rung: choose the label for that half. Third rung: the same task with a time in the morning, before the evening return.

wrong.why: the number looks small or big before the part of the day is thought about
wrong.move: chooses a.m. for any small number and p.m. for any big number
wrong.screen: the card is carried along the strip from midnight to its place, so the child sees which half it lands in, and the clock shows the same hour in both halves

wrong.why: lunch feels like part of the morning when the morning has been busy
wrong.move: puts a lunch box time on a.m. because lunch comes after the morning meal
wrong.screen: the strip is cut at the noon mark in the middle, and a lunch time is carried to the right of that mark and lands on the amber half

wrong.why: the time seems complete once the numbers are down
wrong.move: writes the time with no a.m. or p.m.
wrong.screen: the time card stays open with a small gap after the number and the strip lights both halves, asking which half, until a label is chosen

wrong.why: five seems a morning kind of number
wrong.move: writes a.m. for an evening time that has a small number
wrong.screen: the card is carried along the strip and lands on the amber half, and the label p.m. lights beside it

phases.screen: the day strip with its left half sky blue and its right half amber, and picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football and a dinner plate; the day strip with a picture card, a time card, the number pad, an a.m. button, a p.m. button and a Noon and midnight button
phases.soWhat: from midnight to noon is a.m., and from noon to midnight is p.m. a time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, and noon and midnight are written as words

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the Sun slider crosses the day, the hour hand sweeps round the wall clock and starts again at the twelve in the middle of the strip, and when the sun reaches the far end the sky changes from morning to evening light and then to a moon over the street lamp. On the second phase the sun settles at the middle of the strip with both hands at the twelve and the whole sky glows for a moment.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet placed. On the first phase the day strip is empty from midnight to midnight, the wall clock above it has both hands at the twelve, and a green tag waits empty. On the second a high sun stands over the middle of the strip and a moon over a street lamp stands at each end, with both hands at the twelve. On the third the left half is sky blue and the right half is amber, and picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football and a dinner plate wait beside the strip. On the fourth a picture card stands on the strip with a time card beside it, the number pad, an a.m. button, a p.m. button and a Noon and midnight button. One thing moves, once: the sun gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any time on the pad dropped on the strip, the sun slid from one end to the other, any picture card placed, and the a.m., p.m. and noon and midnight buttons. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the three phases, easy first, on the two rounds of a day, noon and midnight, a.m. and p.m., and writing a time in full, each in a small real scene.
voiceLines: A whole day on one strip, with a sun and a moon.
Turn the hour hand round the clock. How many times does it go round in a day?
Both hands are at the twelve. Is the sun high, or is the moon out?
Is it before noon or after noon? Drop it on its half.
Type the time. Then choose a.m. or p.m., or noon or midnight.
A new time. Find which half of the day it is in.
Free play. Slide the sun and place the times as you like.
Look at where the sun is. Is it before noon or after noon?
You put every time on the right half of the day.

observations.why: a day is two rounds of the hour hand, and the sun crosses the whole strip in a day.
observations.soWhat: a day has 24 hours, because 12 plus 12 is 24.
observations.observe: The hour hand went once round and the sun was only at noon, and it went round again before the sun reached the far end.

observations.why: both are 12 o'clock, one in the day and one at night, and each has its own word.
observations.soWhat: 12 o'clock in the day is noon and 12 o'clock at night is midnight, and neither takes a.m. or p.m.
observations.observe: The twelve of the middle was lit as noon and the twelve of the ends as midnight, and neither had a label.

observations.why: the strip is cut at noon, the sky blue half before it and the amber half after it.
observations.soWhat: from midnight to noon is a.m., and from noon to midnight is p.m.
observations.observe: A card dropped left of the middle took a.m. and a card dropped right of it took p.m.

observations.why: the same clock time falls once in each half of the day.
observations.soWhat: a time is written with a.m. or p.m. after it, and noon and midnight are written as words.
observations.observe: A time typed on the card was not finished until a.m. or p.m. or a word was chosen.

phases.screen: a day strip from one midnight to the next with a wall clock above it and its hour hand waiting at the twelve
phases.win: the second round ends, the day strip fills from end to end and a green tag reads one whole day
phases.traceback: The sun and the red hand go round again, one hour at a time, only as far as the child's own number (1 round: once round, the first half of the strip; 12 hours: 12 cells); a number at or past the answer crosses the day and stops one hour short, so the child finishes the count.
ladder: One round of the hour hand is 12 hours.
Watch the red hand while the marker slides along.
The first box is the rounds and the second is the hours.
Count the rounds, then add up their hours.
Each round has the same hours, so add them.

phases.screen: the day strip with a high sun over the middle and a moon over a street lamp at each end, and both hands at the twelve
phases.win: the middle of the strip lights as noon and the two ends light as midnight, with no label beside them
phases.traceback: The sun is sent along the strip again and stops one hour before the twelve, so the child finishes the slide.
ladder: Both hands are at 12, so the sky must tell you.
Is the sun or the moon out at the 12 you chose?
Is the sun up when the lunch bell rings?
Say what you see in the sky at that 12.
Each of these twelves is written as a word.

phases.screen: the day strip with its left half sky blue and its right half amber, and picture cards of an alarm clock, a school bag, a lunch box, a football and a dinner plate; the day strip with a picture card, a time card, the number pad, an a.m. button, a p.m. button and a Noon and midnight button
phases.win: the card settles in its half and the label a.m. or p.m. lights beside it; the time card is written in full beside the picture and the day strip lights the half it belongs to
phases.traceback: The sun is carried along the strip from midnight to the noon mark and stops there; the time's own place is drawn only at the win.
ladder: Is the evening before noon, or after noon?
Look at the middle mark: noon is there.
Check both the time and the label on the card.
Say what the sky looks like at that time of day.
Blue is the half before noon, and orange is the half after noon.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, no colour means good or bad. The miss empties the answer slot at once (every digit, every box, a picked choice), so it is empty through the traceback; the pad re-opens empty after it.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The sun and the red hand go round again, one hour at a time, only as far as the child's own number (1 round: once round, the first half of the strip; 12 hours: 12 cells); a number at or past the answer crosses the day and stops one hour short, so the child finishes the count.
Phase 2: The sun is sent along the strip again and stops one hour before the twelve, so the child finishes the slide.
Phase 3: The sun is carried along the strip from midnight to the noon mark and stops there; the time's own place is drawn only at the win.

voice.opening: A whole day on one strip, sun and moon.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Slide the marker, or tap a picture to see its time.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: You put every time on the right half of the day.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: The hour hand of the wall clock in the school hall goes once round the clock in 12 hours. How many hours pass while it goes round twice?

question.en: Turn the hour hand twice round the clock: how many hours pass in all?

items.planAnswer: 24 hours, which is one whole day

items.planQuestion: The hour hand of the kitchen wall clock goes once round in 12 hours. How many times does it go round in a whole day?

question.en: Slide the marker across the whole day: how many rounds does the hour hand make?

items.planAnswer: 2 times. A whole day has 24 hours

items.planQuestion: A train leaves the station at one midnight and arrives at the next midnight. How many times does the hour hand of the station clock go round, and how many hours is that?

question.en: Slide the marker from midnight to midnight: how many rounds, and how many hours?

items.planQuestion: In the school kitchen the cook sees both hands of the wall clock pointing straight up to the 12 while the sun is high in the sky. Is it 12 noon or 12 midnight?

question.en: The cook sees both hands at 12 and the sun is high: is it noon or midnight?

items.planAnswer: 12 noon, because the sun is high in the day

items.planQuestion: The moon shines over the street lamp and both hands of the clock point to the 12. Is this time called noon or midnight?

question.en: The moon is out: slide it to the 12 of the night, then press Enter.

items.planAnswer: Midnight, because it is 12 o'clock at night

items.planQuestion: At noon the school lunch bell rings. A child writes noon as 12 and then adds p.m. What should be written instead?

question.en: The lunch bell rings at the highest sun: what is this 12 called?

items.planAnswer: 12 noon. Noon takes no a.m. or p.m.

items.planQuestion: The street lamp outside the school switches on at 5:40 in the evening. Is that a.m. or p.m.?

question.en: The street lamp switches on at 5:40 in the evening: is that a.m., or p.m.?
Ria packs her bag at 7:15 in the morning: drop the card on its half.
Lunch is in the afternoon: type the clock's time, tap the label, then Enter.

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 3 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 3; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 3 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), sun, hour, minute, rounds, placed, label, plainClock, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves
